a283b7927523366d.question: How much did allowing AI tools change task completion time for experienced developers in the METR study?
a283b7927523366d.answer: Allowing AI tools **increased** completion time by 19%—meaning AI tooling slowed developers down [METR, p.1]. This directly contradicted developers' pre-task forecast that AI would *reduce* completion time by 24%, their post-study estimate of a 20% reduction [METR, p.1], and expert forecasts from economists (39% shorter) and ML researchers (38% shorter) [METR, p.1].

bd564fcbed060303.question: What percentage of developers access AI coding tools through personal accounts rather than work-sanctioned ones, according to the Sonar survey?
bd564fcbed060303.answer:
35% of developers access the top 10 AI tools through personal accounts rather than work-sanctioned ones [Sonar, p.14-17].

This varies significantly by tool: 52% of ChatGPT users access it via personal accounts, and 63% of Perplexity users do the same. In contrast, GitHub Copilot and Amazon Q Developer show much lower personal account use at 17% each [Sonar, p.17-18].

6c789f072a018091.question: How did Anthropic's Data Infrastructure team use Claude Code to fix a Kubernetes cluster problem?
6c789f072a018091.answer: When Kubernetes clusters went down and weren't scheduling new pods, the team fed screenshots of dashboards into Claude Code [ClaudeCode, p.1-3]. Claude Code guided them through Google Cloud's UI menu by menu until it identified a warning indicating pod IP address exhaustion [ClaudeCode, p.1-3]. It then provided the exact commands to create a new IP pool and add it to the cluster, resolving the issue without needing to involve networking specialists [ClaudeCode, p.1-3].

707d416a8365c5bd.question: Compare what the METR study measured about AI's effect on developer speed with what developers in the Sonar survey report about AI's impact on their work.
707d416a8365c5bd.answer:
The two sources directly contradict each other. METR's controlled field experiment found that tasks took **19% more time** when developers used AI tools like Cursor Pro—a slowdown effect described as robust across analyses [METR, p.1-2]. Experts and participants also substantially *overestimated* how much AI would help [METR, p.1-2].

By contrast, the Sonar survey of 1,149 professionals found self-reported productivity *gains*: SMB developers reported a **39% increase** in personal productivity, while other developers reported a **34% lift** [Sonar, p.43-45]. Sonar respondents also reported positive impacts on code quality, lower defect rates, and faster time-to-market [Sonar, p.52-53].

The key methodological difference: METR measures *actual task completion times* in real open-source work, while Sonar captures *self-perceived* productivity. The gap likely reflects that developers' subjective sense of being faster diverges significantly from measured outcomes—precisely the inferential problem METR set out to address [METR, p.1-2].
